case.why_ai_cites_it: This is the case that put the word transformative into the middle of American fair use, and nearly every AI training defense is built on the claim that learning statistical relationships from a work is a transformative purpose rather than a substitute for it.

reading.body:
Campbell v. Acuff-Rose, the 1994 case that put the word transformative at the center of American fair use law, is described here as the foundation nearly every AI training defense is built on, the claim that learning statistical relationships from a work is a transformative purpose rather than a substitute for it.

It is cited across the same broad 79-case defense pool as Sega, Kelly, and Google v. Oracle, and quoted directly in two more filings, Sony Music v. Uncharted Labs and X.AI v. Ellison, making it one of the most heavily relied-upon precedents in this entire collection. Its own stated limit is the most consequential in the set. Warhol v. Goldsmith, elsewhere in this collection, later narrowed how far transformative purpose reaches by holding that the first fair-use factor asks whether the new use shares the original's purpose, especially when both are licensed into the same market.

The data does not say how any specific citing case has resolved the tension between Campbell's broad transformative-purpose standard and Warhol's narrower shared-purpose test, only that both are actively in play.
